name: Responses to the Vietnam War
also: the home front, the press, the army, the law, and Hanoi's own response
theatre: United States, mostly; the campuses, the networks, the Congress, the Pentagon

sides.who: the administration until 1968; the 'silent majority' Nixon named in Nov 1969; hard-hat counter-marches (May 1970)
sides.backed: a plurality in polls until roughly mid-1968

sides.who: SDS, the Mobe, the Moratorium, draft resisters, VVAW, the clergy, most of the press after Tet
sides.backed: a majority in polls from roughly mid-1968

chain.did: First teach-in at Michigan (24 Mar 1965); SDS march on Washington (Apr 1965); draft-card burnings; Columbia (1968); after Cambodia, a strike of some four million students, and Kent State (4 May 1970) and Jackson State (15 May 1970).

Cronkite's 'mired in stalemate' broadcast (27 Feb 1968); My Lai reported by Seymour Hersh (Nov 1969); the Pentagon Papers published by the Times and the Post (Jun 1971), upheld by the Supreme Court in seventeen days.

Vietnam Veterans Against the War founded (1967); Winter Soldier hearings in Detroit (Jan–Feb 1971); Dewey Canyon III, medals thrown over the Capitol fence, and John Kerry before the Senate (Apr 1971).

Repealed the Gulf of Tonkin resolution (Jan 1971); Case–Church amendment cutting off funds for combat (Jun 1973); War Powers Resolution over Nixon's veto (Nov 1973); refused Ford's aid request (Apr 1975).
Ended the draft (Jan 1973) for an all-volunteer force; rebuilt doctrine around decisive force and clear objectives, later called the Weinberger–Powell doctrine; stopped using body counts as a metric.
Tet was a military defeat and a political response that worked; the Easter Offensive (1972) tested Vietnamization; the Ho Chi Minh Campaign (1975) answered the ceasefire.
PTSD entered the DSM-III (1980), pushed by veterans' groups; the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, a black wall with 58,000 names and no figures, dedicated 13 Nov 1982.

phases.name: Teach-in
phases.text: Objection is academic and religious; the draft makes it personal; support for the war still holds a majority.

phases.name: The turn
phases.text: Tet, Cronkite, Johnson withdraws (31 Mar 1968), Chicago convention; a majority now calls the war a mistake; the Moratorium (15 Oct 1969) is the largest protest to date.

phases.name: Rupture
phases.text: Cambodia, Kent State, the student strike, Winter Soldier, the Pentagon Papers, the May Day arrests (12,000 in three days).

phases.name: Settlement
phases.text: Draft ends; War Powers; POWs return; Saigon falls; the country argues about the veterans and then builds them a wall.

gauge.unit: Gallup: percent saying it was a mistake to send troops

cost.k: Killed at Kent State and Jackson State

cost.v: 26th Amendment, ratified in 100 days (Jul 1971), the fastest ever, on the argument 'old enough to fight'
War Powers Resolution (1973), still in force and still contested

outcome: The war ended the draft, the president's unilateral war power on paper, the press's deference, and the metric of the body count. It did not end the war; Hanoi did that.
open: Whether the protests shortened the war or, by hardening the 'silent majority', lengthened it — Nixon's own view was that they made withdrawal harder.
Whether Tet changed opinion or merely confirmed a decline already under way since 1967 in the polls.
Whether the all-volunteer force made later wars easier to start because fewer families had a stake.
sources: Kent State: May 4 Collection, Kent State University Libraries
text: A war room of responses to the Vietnam war room: who answered the war, in what order, what it cost them, and what changed in law and doctrine because of it.
